To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Nile rat model of spontaneous type-2 diabetes (T-2-D) recapitulates the five stages of progressive β- cell dysfunction as occurs in human T-2-D and that modification of diet alone prevents the development of T-2-D in this model.
Nile rats fed a chow diet develop the five stages of progressive T2D, whereas those fed a high-fiber, low-fat diet do not develop T2D.

Nile rats fed a high-fiber chow have normoglycemic β-cell compensation and prevent T2D, whereas Nile rats fed chowlaboratory chow develop insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and pancreatic islet dysfunction, recapitulating the five stages of human type 2 diabetes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of the progressive β-cell failure in the Nile rat.
the development of new therapeutic strategies to prevent the progression of β-cell dysfunction in T2D.
understanding the pathophysiology of T2D in a rodent model and the role of dietary fiber in its prevention.

Nile rats are a useful model for T2D, and the diet is a key factor in the development of the disease.
Nile rats are a suitable model of human T2D.
the Nile rat is a suitable animal model for the study of the early events in the development of type 2 diabetic disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Nile rat is a useful model to study the pathophysiology and treatment of T2D.

Nile rats fed a chow diet develop a spontaneous type 2 diabetic phenotype with progressive β-cell dysfunction, whereas Nile rats fed a high-fiber (HF) diet maintain normoglycemic status with increased β-cell mass and function, and that the progression from normoglycemics to diabetics is characterized by the loss of β-cells and a compensatory increase in α-cells.
Nile rats on chow develop T2D, whereas Nile rats on a high-fiber chow diet do not.

Nile rats are a good animal model to study T2D, and the high-fiber diet can be used to prevent or treat the disease in these animals.

the Nile rat model of T2D is useful for investigating the mechanisms of β-cell failure and for evaluating the effects of novel therapeutics on disease progression and reversal.
